li.a: Texas Standard (KUT News): Four men accused in Austin's yogurt shop murders have been exonerated
NBC News: DNA links 3 murders to serial killer who died in 1999
NBC News: 'Yogurt Shop Murders' suspect was possible serial killer now linked to cases across country, police say
FOX 56 Lexington: Timeline suggests Lexington KY woman Linda Rutledge may have been serial killer's last victim
FOX Carolina: Police chief: 'Violent serial rapist and murderer' killed Greenville woman in 1990
Fox News: Texas yogurt shop murders cold case suspect identified after 34 years
A&E: Who Was Robert Eugene Brashers, the Man Behind the Yogurt Shop Murders?

content.p: Robert Eugene Brashers was a man with a long record of violence that police did not connect to one another until after he was dead. He shot himself in a motel in Kennett, Missouri, in January 1999, during a standoff with officers. Almost two decades later, investigators used DNA and ballistic evidence to tie him to a run of rapes and killings across several states, the most notorious of them the 1991 murders of four teenage girls at a yogurt shop in Austin, Texas.

The Austin case had a second, painful chapter. For years, four young men from the city had been charged with the killings, and two of them were convicted before the convictions were overturned. In February 2026 a Travis County judge declared all four innocent. Assistant District Attorney Trudy Strassburger put the matter in one sentence: "The truth is that Robert Eugene Brashers is guilty, and he alone committed the yogurt shop murders."
content.h2: A record that began before the Austin killings
content.p: Brashers was born on 13 March 1958 in Newport News, Virginia, and spent parts of his childhood in Alabama and Indiana, according to A&E. He worked as a bartender, then in construction and HVAC repair, according to the same account. His daughter Deborah later recalled that he seemed like an ordinary father, though she saw warning signs in hindsight.

His first known violent crime came in November 1985 in Florida. Austin police said he made unwanted advances toward a 24-year-old woman. When she turned him down and tried to leave, he shot her in the head and neck. She survived. Fox 56, citing Austin police, reported a 12-year sentence after a guilty plea on a second-degree homicide charge and an aggravated battery count. A&E described the case as an attempted murder conviction. A FOX Carolina timeline said he served three and a half years and was released on 4 May 1989. Fox News reported that he served three years, and NBC News, citing Austin police Detective Daniel Jackson, said he served four.

After his release he moved frequently through the South. Investigators later pieced together a list of places he had been: Georgia, South Carolina, Tennessee, Missouri and Arkansas. In February 1992 he was arrested in Georgia, after police found a stolen pistol and a stolen vehicle, and a radio scanner, a police-style jacket, burglary tools and a fake Tennessee driver's license. He received another prison term and was released in February 1997.
content.h2: The Greenville killing that waited six years for a match
content.p: In April 1990, maintenance workers at an apartment complex in Greenville, South Carolina, found Genevieve "Jenny" Zitricki in her bathtub after she failed to report to work. Greenville police said she had been recently divorced, lived alone, and was known for being outgoing. Her apartment was close to the complex pool, and people often came in to use her bathroom. Sgt. Tim Conroy of the Greenville police said the killer "knew who was in that apartment when he entered." A Greenville police news release gave blunt-force trauma as the cause of death. Investigators later learned she had been sexually assaulted, and the coroner found she had been strangled, according to FOX Carolina.
Greenville police dated the killing to 4 April 1990. NBC News gave 6 April, the day her body was found. Both dates appear in the reporting.

The case stayed open for years. In 2005 Greenville police sent the evidence to SLED for DNA testing. The profile was entered into the national CODIS database, and in 2006 it matched a killing in Missouri that had happened eight years later.

On 11 March 1997, a 14-year-old girl was raped in Memphis, Tennessee. According to NBC News, police said the man came to the door of a house, produced a gun and shoved his way in. A DNA match to that rape was identified in May 2017.

On 28 March 1998, Sherri Scherer, 38, and her 12-year-old daughter Megan were shot dead in their home near Portageville, Missouri. Megan had also been sexually assaulted, the Missouri authorities said. Her father, Anthony Scherer, came home from farm work and found the bodies. Less than three hours later, a man tried to force his way into a home in Dyersburg, Tennessee, and shot a woman during a struggle. She survived. NBC News reports that she was shot in the arm; FOX Carolina reports that she was shot through the door of her mobile home. Ballistics tests showed the same gun was used in both attacks.

In 1998 a Lexington, Kentucky, woman named Linda Rutledge was killed in a shooting and a structure fire. Her death stayed unsolved for 27 years. In 2025 Austin police said the .380 casing from the Yogurt Shop drain matched a weapon used in the 1998 Lexington killing. FOX 56 reported that the Kentucky link had not been known until then, and that investigators have urged authorities to take another look at similar cold cases.
content.h2: The Yogurt Shop murders in Austin
content.p: On the night of 6 December 1991, shortly before midnight, an Austin patrol officer saw flames at the I Can't Believe It's Yogurt! shop. Firefighters put out the blaze and found the bodies of Eliza Thomas, 17, Amy Ayers, 13, and the sisters Jennifer Harbison, 17, and Sarah Harbison, 15. Jennifer and Eliza worked at the shop. Sarah and Amy had come along to be picked up for a sleepover.

Austin police said all four girls had been shot, bound and gagged. Police said all of the girls except Eliza Thomas had been sexually assaulted. The fire damage and water from the sprinkler system made the evidence hard to collect. Police later said there were "thousands of tips and dozens of 'confessions,'" but no arrests were made for years. Fox News put the number of potential suspects over the years at more than 1,200, and said false confessions were common.

In 1999 police arrested four young men from the Austin area: Forrest Welborn, Maurice Pierce, Michael Scott and Robert Springsteen. Springsteen and Scott signed confessions that implicated themselves and, in different ways, the others. Both later said those confessions were false and had been coerced after hours of questioning. The reporting disagrees on the convictions. KUT says Springsteen and Scott were convicted of murder in 1999; A&E and Fox News say the convictions came in 2001 and 2002. In each version, Springsteen was sentenced to death and Scott to life in prison.

The prosecutions did not hold. Both convictions were thrown out on appeal, one of the reasons being that one defendant's confession had been used against the others during the trial. KUT reports that the state's highest criminal court threw out both convictions in 2006; A&E gives 2006 for Springsteen and 2007 for Scott. DNA evidence excluded Springsteen and Scott from biological material taken from beneath one victim's fingernails, and no DNA matched any of the four men. In 2009, A&E reports, all charges against Springsteen and Scott were dismissed.

KUT says Pierce was held in jail for more than three years before trial, and that his case was dismissed in 2003. Welborn's charges were dropped in 2000, according to KUT, while A&E says neither Pierce nor Welborn was ever brought to trial. Pierce was 15 when he was arrested, his daughter Marisa told the court in 2026. KUT says he was shot by an Austin police officer in 2010, after a mental health episode in which he tried to stab the officer. A&E gives a different account: that he struck the officer with his vehicle during a traffic stop.

By 2018 the Greenville case, the Missouri killings and the Memphis rape had been connected through the national DNA database. Investigators in several agencies then turned to a private company, Parabon NanoLabs, which combines DNA testing with genetic genealogy. NBC News reported that investigators obtained DNA samples from Brashers' relatives. The company's analysis pointed to Brashers. Because he was dead, investigators then had his body exhumed and took DNA from it. Fox 56 says the exhumation was ordered by a court. A&E says the body was taken from an Arkansas cemetery. The DNA from his remains matched the DNA found at the crime scenes.

Greenville police chief Ken Miller said: "Today is a bittersweet moment, in that we can finally bring closure to the family of Jenny Zitricki." He said generations of detectives who worked the case "can now see this case closed." The Greenville department paid for the exhumation because it needed a DNA match taken directly from Brashers' body. Miller described Brashers as a "violent serial rapist and murderer." Zitricki's brother, Philip Hegedusichi, said his sister was "a force of nature."

The standoff took place at a Super 8 motel in Kennett, Missouri. A FOX Carolina timeline dates it to 13 January 1999, when officers found a vehicle in the motel parking lot and, after about four hours of negotiation, found Brashers hiding under a bed with a gun. NBC News reported that the standoff began when Kennett police sought to question him about a stolen license plate, and that he was not a suspect in the killings or the rape at that time. Fox News reported that he had been hiding at the motel with his wife, daughter and two stepdaughters, and had released them before the end. A&E gives 19 January 1999 as the date of his death, and says he shot himself with a .380 handgun rather than surrender.

Investigators at the time believed they had closed the case on a violent fugitive. They had no reason to connect him to the Greenville killing, the Memphis rape, the Missouri murders, or the Lexington death. That changed when the DNA databases caught up.

In 2022 Austin police gave the Yogurt Shop case to a new detective, Daniel Jackson. Austin police later said the .380 cartridge recovered from a drain inside the shop had not been submitted to the national ballistic database for many years, and that the software had since improved. In June 2025 it was submitted, and it produced a match to the weapon used in the 1998 Lexington killing. Jackson then asked labs across the country that do Y-STR DNA testing to search their profiles, and a South Carolina lab reported a match to the 1990 Greenville killing.

On 26 September 2025, Austin police publicly named Brashers as the killer. Austin police said the .380 pistol Brashers had when a Border Patrol checkpoint stopped him had the same serial number as the gun he used in his suicide. Brashers had been stopped there less than 48 hours after the murders, driving a stolen car from Georgia. Fox News reported that the HBO documentary series about the case had premiered the month before. Brashers' daughter Deborah told reporters she had not known about the killings, and said her father was a contractor who worked in construction for a while.

In February 2026, Travis County Judge Dayna Blazey formally declared the four men innocent. The District Attorney, José Garza, had filed a motion to revisit the case in late 2025. Garza apologized to the men and their families at the hearing. Michael Scott, who was the only one of the four to speak in court, said: "I am not guilty." Robert Springsteen said in a written statement read by his lawyer that he had been "persecuted every day." A&E reports that Pierce did not live to see his name cleared.
content.h2: What the record does and does not settle
content.p: Police say DNA and ballistic evidence link Brashers to killings in Austin, Greenville, Portageville and Lexington, and to the Memphis rape. He is not on trial for any of them, and no court has heard the evidence against him. Austin police said no physical evidence from the scene was ever linked to any of the four men first accused. Some details still differ between accounts: the dates of the Greenville killing, the length of the 1985 sentence, the years of the Springsteen and Scott convictions, the date of the Kennett standoff, and the way the Dyersburg victim was shot. Where the accounts disagree, each version is attributed to its source.
